title: Primer length payoff - latency & cost portrait (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This memo captures exploratory benchmarks on how primer length (system prompt + few-shot context) and priming strategies (static prefix vs example-append vs dynamic prefill) affect observed latency, token cost, and effective per-request economics on our hosted runtime. Goal is not a final SLA change proposal but to seed operational tradeoffs for prompt engineering guidance, default SDK behavior, and potential runtime caching heuristics.

Experiment summary (short):
- Models: rwv1-13B, rwv2-30B-quant (int8), and a larger 70B float baseline to anchor throughput.
- Workload: conversational completions with client messages ~40-80 tokens, varying primer lengths: 0, 64, 256, 1024 primer tokens.
- Priming modes: static-prefix (same primer persisted in request), few-shot-append (examples appended per request), dynamic-prefill (server-side KV prefill kept in session cache).
- Metrics: p50/p95 generation latency (ms), end-to-end request latency (ms), tokens billed (request primer tokens included in billed context for hosted API), per-request cost estimate (USD), and cache hit fraction for dynamic-prefill.

Method and environment:
- Hardware: dedicated A100-like baseline (single GPU), and a quantized inference machine (V100-like for int8 path).
- Batching: two modes tested: small-window (max batch size 4, latency-target 150ms) and opportunistic (max batch size 32, latency-target 500ms).
- Cold vs warm: cold = fresh process/container, no KV cache; warm = after steady-state 5-minute warmup with representative traffic.
- Billing assumptions (approx): $0.000012 per token for rwv1-13B float, $0.000009 per token for 30B-quant. (internal unit costs for illustrative economics).

Key findings (high level):
1) Primer length increases token billing linearly but the incremental latency per extra primer token is sublinear when KV caching is effective.
   - Example: for rwv1-13B under warm dynamic-prefill, moving from 64 -> 256 primer tokens raised billed tokens by ~192 tokens but increased p95 latency by only ~12-18ms because prefix tokens were reused via KV hits.
2) Static-prefix and few-shot-append both inflate latency and cost proportionally to primer size when no session cache is available. Few-shot-append is worse in batching scenarios because appended examples increase batch memory footprint and reduce batch throughput.
3) Dynamic-prefill with a modest session cache (kv hit rate > 0.7) yields the best cost/latency tradeoff for repeated conversational flows — but requires session affinity and cache eviction tuning.
4) Quantized models reduce per-token compute cost but have slightly higher single-request latency variance in small-batch (<8) regimes.

Representative numbers (rwv1-13B, opportunistic batching, warm):
- Primer 0 tokens: p50 latency = 120ms, p95 = 220ms, billed tokens = 120, cost (USD) = 0.00144
- Primer 64 tokens static: p50 = 150ms, p95 = 310ms, billed tokens = 184, cost = 0.00221
- Primer 256 tokens static: p50 = 210ms, p95 = 420ms, billed tokens = 368, cost = 0.00442
- Primer 256 tokens dynamic-prefill (kv hit 0.8): p50 = 165ms, p95 = 238ms, billed tokens = 368 (billed) but effective compute tokens saved equivalent to ~120 tokens of reused compute due to cache -> effective compute-cost approx 0.0030

ASCII chart: p95 latency vs primer length (rwv1-13B, warm, opportunistic)
Primer tokens | p95 latency (ms)
0      | ######################## 220
64     | ######################################## 310
256    | ######################################################## 420
1024   | ########################################################################## 620

Notes on that chart: bars are visualized; slope steepness increases beyond ~512 tokens as attention matrices force extra kernel paths and memory pressure starts to kick in.

Batching and slot utilization observations:
- Small-window mode preserves lower p50 but suffers from per-token cost due to less aggregation benefits. Adding primer tokens in small-window often increases end-to-end latency more than in opportunistic mode because batch size cannot amortize prefix compute.
- Opportunistic batching absorbs primer work better: when primer is identical across requests, batching shares prefix compute and memory, improving throughput. But when primer varies per-request, batching is less beneficial and can cause tail latency due to stragglers.

Cold start / container churn effects:
- Cold sessions without prefill show a 2x p95 penalty for large primers (256+) compared to warm. This suggests an operational leaky bucket: primers amplify cold-start stress.

Quantization and model variant tradeoffs:
- 30B-quant reduces nominal per-token cost ~25% vs 13B float in our unit pricing, but in small-batch, p95 increased by ~30ms (due to slower int8 kernels on our chosen GPU and extra dequant steps). For sustained throughput (batch >= 16), quantized path regained advantage.

Recommendations (practical):
1) Encourage SDK defaults to prefer dynamic-prefill (session-level preloads) for conversational flows where primer is stable across turns. Provide an opt-in pattern: Session.prefill(primer_id).
2) For one-off few-shot prompts (examples that change per request), limit appended examples to ~3 examples or provide an example-reduction transform (curation + heuristic truncation) in the client SDK before sending.
3) Expose a "primer-cost-estimate" quick API in console that shows billed token delta for a given primer and projects p95 impact under current region capacity. Helps CS and customers reason.
4) Runtime: track per-session kv-hit-rate, evictions, and priming-induced cold-starts as first-class metrics and surface them on Console as "primer efficiency".
5) For Dedicated plans, provide an autoscaling rule template tuned to primer-heavy workloads: keep a small warm pool with session affinity, and scale aggressively on queue depth for large-primer spikes.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How do multi-turn long-range attention optimizations (e.g., sliding window) interact with long primers older than 1024 tokens? We should run a sweep with 2k+ primers focusing on memory churn.
- Investigate hybrid approach: upload canonical large primer once and reference by ID (server-side stable prefill storage) to remove billing duplication for static corpora. Need policy + security review.
- Run customer-facing cost-sensitivity examples for a few customers (support case cohort) to validate recommended SDK priming patterns before making Console changes.

Appendix A: micro-table (p50/p95/compute-effective-savings)
Primer|p50(ms)|p95(ms)|billed_tokens|approx_cost(USD)|effective_compute_saved_tokens
0     |120    |220    |120          |0.00144          |0
64    |150    |310    |184          |0.00221          |0
256S  |210    |420    |368          |0.00442          |0
256D  |165    |238    |368          |0.00442 (billed) |~120
1024D |360    |620    |1144         |0.0137           |~600 (if kv_hit 0.85)

Appendix B: recommended doc links and tickets
- Follow-up perf sweep: JIRA-INF-4509 (primer-2k-sweep)
- SDK feature: RFC for Session.prefill API: git PR #987

Draft notes / to do for next version:
- Add graphs with region breakdown (US vs eu-west) and instance-type (A100 vs T4)
- Add cost per effective compute token metric (normalize billed tokens vs actual compute cycles measured by GPU kernels)
- Validate numbers against Dedicated cluster (not just hosted)

Notes to self: this doc is intentionally qualitative and rough; share with Lina and Ramesh, schedule 30-min sync to prioritize which recommendations to convert into concrete RFCs.

-- Ava
